taciturn

/TAS-ih-turn/ - the stress falls on TAS · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Taciturn means not inclined to talk.

The lighthouse suited Wren, taciturn since childhood, who could pass an entire supply run with the boat's captain in comfortable silence.

Example

Mr. Abernathy has taught geometry for thirty years on perhaps ten sentences a day: he writes the proof, taps the crucial step twice, and waits. Students call him taciturn; his classes are also the quietest and highest-scoring in the building.

Taciturn describes a person's habit, not a mood: the taciturn are sparing with words year-round, by temperament rather than shyness or anger. Someone quiet at one party is just quiet; someone quiet at every party, every meeting, every dinner is taciturn.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tight-lipped: Tight-lipped is silence on purpose, usually about one particular subject—press a tight-lipped witness and you feel the door held shut. Taciturn silence guards nothing; it is a year-round temperament of spending few words on every subject. Tight-lipped protects a secret; taciturn is simply how the person runs.

uncommunicative: Uncommunicative means giving little away by any channel—short answers, no updates, unreturned messages—and it is usually felt as a problem by the people left waiting. Taciturn is narrower and kinder: a settled habit of using few words, with no suggestion that information is being withheld.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

talkative: full of easy, flowing conversation

chatty: bubbling with small talk

Where it sits · how rarely words get spent

quiet → taciturn → silent

quiet vs. taciturn: Quiet is the milder, roomier word and claims much less than taciturn—a quiet guest still chats when a topic lands close to home, while a taciturn one stays sparing with words all evening, every evening.

silent vs. taciturn: Silent goes further than quiet—the silent monk says nothing at all by vow, while the taciturn one simply spends words like rare coins.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — tacit: silent, unspoken (Latin tacitus, from tacere, 'to be silent')

Suffix — -urn: of that character (Latin -urnus, as in nocturnus)

Put it together: Tacit- (silent, from Latin tacere, 'to be silent') + -urn (of that character, Latin -urnus) = of a silent character. Latin taciturnus described the habitually silent, and English took it over unchanged in meaning: the taciturn don't refuse to speak—they just seldom see the need.

Use the root in a new word: tacit: You met tacit earlier in this course - as in the tacit truce the two rivals kept all season.

Word Choice

neutral

Taciturn is for people whose words are permanently rationed—a temperament, not a sulk. Unit-mates split the nearby ground: aloof is distance of manner (an aloof person may chat politely and still hold you off); bashful and diffident go quiet from embarrassment or self-doubt; stolid keeps feeling—rather than words—off the record. If the silence is a one-day mood, 'quiet' or 'tight-lipped' serves better.
